title: Data annotations and the Fluent API
summary: Two ways to configure the same model, when to use each, and IEntityTypeConfiguration.

steps.title: Two ways to say the same thing
body: **Data annotations** are attributes on the entity class. **The Fluent API** is code in the context's `OnModelCreating`. They configure the same model:

Annotations sit next to the property and read well, but they only cover the common cases and they put database details into your domain class. The Fluent API can express **everything** (composite indexes, check constraints, conversions, relationships in detail) and keeps the entity a plain class.
When both configure the same thing, **the Fluent API wins**: EF Core applies conventions, then annotations, then `OnModelCreating`.

steps.prompt: Match each annotation to its Fluent API twin.
steps.explain: Every annotation has a Fluent API equivalent. The reverse is not true: many Fluent options have no attribute.

code: protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=library.db");
steps.explain: The annotation set 50, then `OnModelCreating` set 120: the Fluent API is applied last, so it wins. The column name came only from the annotation, so it stays `name`. `db.Model` is the model EF Core built, and you can inspect it like this.

steps.title: Keeping OnModelCreating tidy
body: One `OnModelCreating` for fifty entities becomes a wall of code. Move each entity's configuration into its own class with `IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>`:
In a real project, `model.ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly(typeof(LibraryDb).Assembly)` finds every configuration class at once.

steps.explain: The interface is `IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>`, its one method receives an `EntityTypeBuilder<T>`, and lengths are set with `HasMaxLength`.

steps.prompt: Your entities live in a domain project that must not depend on EF Core. How do you configure them?
options: With the Fluent API (or IEntityTypeConfiguration classes) in the data project
With data annotations on the entities
You cannot: EF Core requires attributes
By renaming the properties to match the conventions
steps.explain: The Fluent API lives with the context, so the entity classes stay plain C# with no EF Core references. That is a common reason teams prefer it. (A few annotations like `[MaxLength]` come from `System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations`, not EF Core, but the EF-specific ones like `[Index]` do not.)

code: protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=library.db");
protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder model) => model.ApplyConfiguration(new BookConfig());
steps.explain: `ToTable` renames the table from the `DbSet` name to `Catalogue`, and `Ignore` keeps `Rating` out of the database, just like `[NotMapped]`.

steps.title: Configure it fluently
prompt: The tests give you this entity, with **no** attributes:
The tests apply your class in their context's `OnModelCreating`.
template: Dojo.Check("the table is LibraryMembers", dojoSql.Contains("CREATE TABLE \"LibraryMembers\""), dojoSql);
Dojo.Check("Number is the primary key", dojoSql.Contains("\"Number\" INTEGER NOT NULL CONSTRAINT \"PK_LibraryMembers\" PRIMARY KEY"), dojoSql);
Dojo.Check("Email is required", dojoSql.Contains("\"Email\" TEXT NOT NULL"), dojoSql);
Dojo.Eq("Name has a maximum length of 80", 80, dojoDb.Model.FindEntityType(typeof(Member))?.FindProperty("Name")?.GetMaxLength());
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=club.db");
protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder model) => model.ApplyConfiguration(new MemberConfig());
